meta.name: Steel
meta.definition: The steel industry covers the production of crude and finished steel from iron ore, coking coal and scrap through blast-furnace/BOF, DRI-EAF and scrap-EAF routes, and its downstream use in construction, infrastructure, automotive, engineering and consumer goods.

summary.headline: India is now the world's second-largest crude steel producer (168.4 MT in FY2025-26) and the fastest-growing large steel market globally, with finished steel consumption at 163.7 MT and capacity crossing 220 MTPA on the way to a 300 MTPA target by 2030-31
key_takeaways: India's crude steel production hit 168.4 MT and finished steel consumption 163.7 MT in FY2025-26, growing 9-11% versus a stagnant-to-declining global market led by China's slowdown

Construction and infrastructure absorb roughly 60-68% of India's steel, making government capex (₹12.2 lakh crore FY26-27) and projects like Bharatmala and PM Gati Shakti the single biggest demand lever

The market is a two-tier structure: five to six large integrated producers (Tata Steel, JSW Steel, SAIL, JSPL, AM/NS India) account for ~59% of crude steel output, with a large fragmented secondary/EAF sector filling the rest

India remains heavily import-dependent on coking coal (80-90% imported, mostly from Australia) even as it turned a marginal net exporter of finished steel in FY26, helped by a new 12% safeguard duty against cheap Chinese/Asian imports

Government policy (PLI for specialty steel, National Steel Policy 2030-31 target of 300 MTPA capacity and 158kg per-capita consumption, Green Steel Taxonomy) is the key structural driver, alongside continuing dependence on imported inputs and Chinese oversupply risk
summary.report_markdown:
## Market size and trajectory
India's finished steel consumption rose from 77 MT in FY2014-15 to 163.7 MT in FY2025-26 (+7.6% YoY), while finished steel production reached 160.9 MT (+9.7% YoY) and crude steel production hit 168.4 MT (+10.7% YoY) — the best-ever fiscal year for the sector. India's crude steel capacity has crossed 220 MTPA (up from 198.5 MT the prior year), moving toward the National Steel Policy's 300 MTPA target by 2030-31 and a longer-term 500 MT ambition by 2047. India overtook Japan in 2018 to become the world's second-largest crude steel producer and is the world's second-largest steel consumer; China remains far larger (960.8-1,005 MT) but its output has been flat-to-declining, while India posted the highest growth (6.3-7.1%) among top-10 producers in recent years.

## Segments
Construction and infrastructure account for roughly 60-68% of steel demand, engineering/packaging ~22%, and automobiles ~9%. By product form, flat steel holds slightly over half the market (54.2% share in 2025) versus long steel, driven by automotive and manufacturing; structural steel leads by product category (33.6%). By technology, the BF-BOF (blast furnace) route accounts for ~44-46% of output versus EAF/other routes, with EAF share expected to rise on scrap availability and specialty long products. Regionally, Odisha, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh together supply over half of India's crude steel (with Odisha the single largest producing state), while West & Central India (34.7% share) and North India are the largest consuming regions.

## Growth drivers
- **Infrastructure and government capex**: FY26-27 capex budget of ₹12.2 lakh crore (3x FY19-20 levels), Bharatmala, PM Gati Shakti, metro rail expansion (1,036+ km across 24 cities) and PMAY housing (4+ crore houses sanctioned)
- **Automotive**: 28+ million vehicles produced in FY2024-25, rising AHSS/EV-grade steel demand as India becomes a top-3 global auto hub
- **Policy push**: National Steel Policy 2017 targets, PLI Scheme for Specialty Steel (₹6,322 crore outlay, 42+ MoUs, ~24 MT specialty capacity created), Mission Coking Coal, Green Steel Taxonomy
- **Urbanisation**: urban population projected to reach 600-630 million by 2030

## Value chain and India's import dependence
India has large captive iron ore reserves (Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka; potential 700 MT/year output, world's 4th-largest iron ore producer) giving domestic steelmakers a raw-material cost edge. However, India remains structurally short of coking coal — importing 55-90% of requirements (mostly from Australia, also Russia, US, Mozambique) — exposing producers to global price swings; the government's Mission Coking Coal targets raising domestic raw coking coal output to 140 MT by FY2029-30 to cut import dependence from 85% to 65% by 2030-31. About 30 MT of steel scrap is consumed annually, of which ~5 MT is imported.

## Trade, tariffs and China risk
India swung between net importer and net exporter status through FY24-26: it was briefly a net importer in FY2023-24/FY2024-25 as cheap Chinese, Vietnamese and other Asian steel flowed in (Chinese exports priced USD 50-100/tonne below domestic steel amid Chinese oversupply), then turned a marginal net exporter again in FY2025-26 (net exports of 0.08 MT) as exports rose 35.8% and imports fell 46.5%. In April 2025 India imposed a 12% provisional safeguard duty (tapering to 11% over three years) on select flat steel products to counter import surges, alongside anti-dumping duties historically targeted at China, Russia and Ukraine, a revamped Steel Import Monitoring System (SIMS 2.0/SARAL-SIMS), 143+ Quality Control Orders covering 723 products, and a 'melt and pour' rule requiring steel to be fully manufactured in India to qualify as domestic for government procurement.

## Players and market structure
The top-6 producers (SAIL, RINL, Tata Steel Group, AM/NS India, JSW Steel, JSPL) produced ~59% of India's crude steel in FY24, with the private sector accounting for 81-83% of total output. JSW Steel is the largest private producer (capacity heading to 50 MT by 2030, ₹2 lakh crore+ investment planned) and has the highest projected sales-volume growth among peers; Tata Steel is the most globally diversified (Europe, Thailand operations) with 100% captive iron ore; SAIL is the largest state-owned integrated producer (~19-20 MT capacity, expanding to 35 MT by 2031) but lags peers on margins and growth; JSPL is expanding fastest (up to 65% capacity growth) and posts the best EBITDA margins among listed peers.

## Margins and cost pressures
Industry EBITDA margins compressed sharply from FY22 highs due to falling steel prices and elevated coking coal costs, before an expected recovery from FY26 onward; JSPL consistently leads on margin and least leverage, SAIL lags with the weakest EBITDA/tonne among tier-I mills. High logistics costs (13-14% of GDP), import-dependent coking coal, and volatile international steel prices remain persistent cost headwinds, partly offset by rising value-added product mix (>50% of sales for most large integrated players).

sections.heading: Executive summary
prose: India is now the world's second-largest crude steel producer, making 168.4 MT in FY2025-26, and is the fastest-growing large steel market globally. Finished steel consumption reached 163.7 MT in the same year, and installed capacity has crossed 220 MTPA on its way to a government target of 300 MTPA by 2030-31.

Growth is running at 9-11% a year, far ahead of a stagnant-to-declining global steel market that is being dragged down by China's slowdown. Construction and infrastructure remain the biggest demand driver, absorbing roughly 60-68% of India's steel, backed by record government capital spending.

The industry is a two-tier market: five to six large integrated producers control about 59% of crude steel output, while a large, fragmented secondary and electric-arc-furnace (EAF) sector fills the rest. India still depends on imports for 80-90% of its coking coal, but it briefly turned a net exporter of finished steel in FY2025-26, helped by a new 12% safeguard duty against cheap Chinese and Asian imports.

sections.heading: Market size & growth
prose: India's finished steel consumption reached 163.7-164.36 MT in FY2025-26 (2026), up from 152.13 MT in 2025 and 136.29 MT in 2024. This continues a steady multi-year climb from 100.17 MT in 2020 and 94.89 MT in 2021, through 105.75 MT in 2022 and 119.89 MT in 2023.

The trend shows consistent, accelerating growth over the past five years, with India adding roughly 12-16 MT of consumption a year in the most recent period. This growth stands out globally: India is the only top-10 steel producer posting double-digit volume growth while China, Japan and the EU stagnate or decline.

sections.heading: Segments
prose: Construction and infrastructure are the dominant end-use segment, accounting for about 68% of total steel consumption in FY2023-24 (other estimates put it at 60-65%). Engineering and packaging make up around 22%, and the automobile industry accounts for about 9%, though this is expected to rise as India's auto sector grows.

By product form, flat steel led with 54.2% of the market in 2025, reflecting strong automotive and manufacturing demand. By product category, structural steel held the largest share at 33.6%. On production technology, the blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) route accounted for 46.12% of 2025 output, though EAF capacity is expected to gain ground as scrap availability improves.

Geographically, West and Central India is the largest consuming region, with a 34.7% share in 2025. On the supply side, secondary steel plants including MSMEs made up 47% of crude steel capacity in FY25, alongside the large integrated primary producers.

sections.heading: Value chain
prose: The value chain starts with raw material sourcing: iron ore is concentrated in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Goa, where India has captive reserves supporting up to 700 MT of annual production potential. Coking coal, by contrast, is heavily import-dependent (80-90%), sourced mainly from Australia and also Russia, the US and Mozambique. Producers with 100% captive iron ore, such as Tata Steel, achieve the highest EBITDA per tonne in the industry, while coking coal import dependence remains the key cost-volatility risk.

Crude steel production is concentrated in Odisha, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh, which together account for over half of national output, using either the BF-BOF route or electric arc furnaces. Integrated BF-BOF players generally achieve lower unit costs at scale than secondary or EAF producers.

Midstream processing converts crude steel into finished flat and long products, including hot-rolled coils, cold-rolled sheets, galvanised and coated products, and specialty steels. Value-added and coated or specialty products carry higher margins than commodity long products. Finished steel then moves through a distribution network of traders, stockists and service centres that ensure last-mile availability to end-users and downstream fabricators.

sections.heading: Distribution & channels
prose: Steel reaches end-users through several channels: direct sales, steel service centres, distributors and dealers, and a growing online channel. SAIL alone has built a countrywide network of over 2,300 dealers to ensure availability across virtually all districts.
Exports are also a significant channel: Indian steel is retailed through more than 9,500 outlets domestically and exported to over a hundred countries worldwide.

sections.heading: Key players & positioning
prose: The market is led by a handful of large integrated producers. JSW Steel is India's largest private-sector steel producer with about 16.9% market share and roughly 28-30 MT of capacity, targeting 50 MT by 2030; it is also the largest exporter of coated products from India. Tata Steel holds about 11.9% share, benefits from 100% captive iron ore giving it industry-leading EBITDA per tonne, and plans to double domestic capacity from 21 MT to 40 MT by FY30.

SAIL, the largest state-owned producer with about 14.8% share, is expanding capacity from around 21 MT to 35 MT by FY31 but lags private peers on EBITDA per tonne and growth; its market share is expected to fall below 10% by FY30 as faster-growing private players gain ground. Jindal Steel & Power (JSPL) is expanding capacity by 65% via its Angul, Odisha project to 15.9 MT by FY26-27, which will make it the fourth-largest steel manufacturer in India; it consistently leads peers on EBITDA margin and carries the least leverage. AM/NS India, a joint venture of ArcelorMittal and Nippon Steel, holds about 5.2% share and is building a new 7 MTPA plant in Andhra Pradesh.

Other notable players include Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited (RINL), the second-largest public-sector steelmaker with 6.3 MT capacity and India's largest rail supplier; NMDC Steel, recently demerged and building a greenfield plant at Nagarnar; Jindal Stainless, the leading stainless steel producer in India and globally; and downstream tube and pipe makers APL Apollo Tubes and JTL Industries. Bhushan Power & Steel, once one of India's largest secondary steelmakers, was acquired by JSW Steel via insolvency proceedings for Rs 19,700 crore. Globally, China Baowu Group, ArcelorMittal and Ansteel Group are the top three steel producers by market share, though this is a global rather than India-specific context.

sections.heading: Supply & capacity
prose: India's total steel capacity stood at 220.4 MT in 2026, with capacity utilisation running at about 80%. Among major producers, JSW Steel had 29.7 MT of capacity in FY24, growing toward 51.5 MT by FY30-31; Tata Steel had 35.3 MT (domestic plus international); SAIL had 21.4 MT, expanding to 35 MT by FY31; and JSPL had 9.6 MT, expanding to 15.9 MT by FY26-27.
Finished steel imports fell from 9.55 million tonnes in 2024 to 6.52 million tonnes in 2025, partly reflecting the new safeguard duty on select flat steel products.

sections.heading: Tailwinds vs headwinds
prose: Tailwinds include India's standout double-digit volume growth among top-10 global producers, a brief turn to net exporter status in FY2025-26 (trade surplus of 0.08 MT, with exports up 35.8% and imports down 46.5% year-on-year), and domestic iron ore self-sufficiency across Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka that gives producers a raw-material cost edge. The government's 12% safeguard duty on select flat steel products, imposed in April 2025, is also protecting domestic mills from import surges, and overall Indian steel demand has grown at 6.4-11.6% CAGR versus flat-to-declining global demand.

Headwinds include heavy reliance on imported coking coal (80-90%, mostly from Australia), which exposes producers to global price and currency volatility, and persistent pricing pressure from Chinese exports sold USD 50-100 per tonne below domestic steel. India's per-capita steel consumption of about 93-98 kg remains well below the global average of 209-230 kg, limiting near-term per-person demand upside. Lower-tier producers like SAIL face margin pressure and market-share loss to faster-growing private players. High logistics costs (13-14% of GDP) and the distance of eastern India's steel plants from demand centres raise delivered costs, and India briefly slipped back to net importer status in April-July FY27 as imports rose 36.6% year-on-year, outpacing 35% export growth.

sections.heading: Outlook
prose: India's steel industry is set to keep outgrowing the rest of the world, supported by record government capital expenditure (₹12.2 lakh crore for FY2026-27), the National Steel Policy's target of 300 MTPA capacity and 255 MT production by 2030-31, and a longer-term goal of 500 MT capacity by 2047. The PLI Scheme for Specialty Steel is expected to lift specialty steel output to 42 MT by 2026-27, while rising vehicle production and urbanisation (India's urban population is expected to reach 600-630 million by 2030) should broaden demand beyond construction into automotive and consumer segments.

The main risks to this outlook are structural: continued heavy dependence on imported coking coal, the constant threat of low-priced Chinese steel exports, and the volatility of trade flows, as shown by India's swing from net exporter to net importer within the same fiscal year. Government trade defences such as the safeguard duty and domestic quality-control orders will remain important tools to manage these pressures as capacity expands toward the 2030-31 targets.

margins.notes: Industry EBITDA margins peaked around FY22 on strong post-COVID realisations, then fell sharply through FY23-25 on soft prices and high coking coal costs.
